sentences.text: [Name of our group, who we represent, and how many families we are in touch with.]

sections.heading: Why we are writing to you

sentences.text: We are writing because HNRNPU-related epileptic encephalopathy and SLC6A1-related epilepsy with myoclonic-atonic seizures are both recorded on the same broad mechanism road: too little protein from one lost copy, with loss of function inferred for each condition.
The phenotype similarity score between the two conditions is marked high.
Shared informative features listed in the pack include atonic seizure, absence-type non-motor seizure, non-motor seizure, dialeptic seizure, and myoclonus.
The gene-disease link is marked definitive for both HNRNPU and SLC6A1 in Gene2Phenotype.
Both conditions have patient organizations listed in the pack.
Both conditions also have registry or natural history routes listed.
Both conditions have disease models reported in PubMed.
The pack says registry design and natural history protocol are transferable between these communities.
The pack also says outcome measures and endpoints are transferable, but age of onset and severity still need review before any instrument is adopted.
The pack says the clinical network, sites, and investigators may also be transferable.

sections.heading: What we would like to learn from or reuse

sentences.text: We would like to learn from the SLC6A1 natural history and registry work, including NCT07531511, Simons Searchlight, Citizen Health, and the SLC6A1 Connect registry listing.
We would like to compare data items, consent language, visit schedules, and measured domains, because the pack says these parts are likely to carry over.
We would also like to understand whether your community's clinical network could help point us to experienced sites and investigators.
For therapeutic strategy, disease models, and trial design, the pack says these are not ready to copy directly and need expert review first.
The pack found no active NIH-funded HNRNPU projects in FY2025-2026, while it found two for SLC6A1.
The pack found no targeted clinical trial for HNRNPU, but it found targeted SLC6A1 trials at gene level.
We must not assume that an SLC6A1 animal or cell model can stand in for HNRNPU, because the pack says those models are gene-specific.
We must not assume that any family shares the same mechanism just because the two conditions are on the same road.
The pack says mechanism is recorded per gene and disease, not per family, and a child's own variant may act differently.
Because of that, each family's variant class should be confirmed with a clinical geneticist before acting on any transfer idea.
The pack also says the curated mechanism for both conditions is inferred from variant types rather than functional evidence.
The SLC6A1 organization listing passed only an automated check of its own site, and no human verification is recorded in the pack.
Has our child's specific HNRNPU variant been functionally classified as loss of function, gain of function, or dominant negative, and does it match the mechanism recorded for the condition.
What functional evidence exists for HNRNPU, since the curated mechanism in the pack is inferred from variant types rather than direct functional studies.
Is SLC6A1 Connect the right contact for this community, and does it run a registry.
Which registry fields, consent elements, visit schedules, and outcome measures from the SLC6A1 studies are the safest to reuse for HNRNPU.
If trial planning is discussed, which parts of SLC6A1 trial design are reasonable templates, and which parts should not be carried over without new evidence.
